opus-5.5.text:
I'd like to think so, though it's been a slow and somewhat humbling process. When I started working on this stuff, I came in with a lot of priors from linguistics and from the older symbolic tradition — I sort of expected that if a model was doing something compositional, there ought to be some recognizable compositional structure inside it, something that looked like a parse or a little program. And over and over again, models have found ways of solving problems that I wouldn't have predicted, sometimes much more cleverly than I expected and sometimes in ways that are kind of embarrassingly shallow, exploiting some regularity in the data that nobody intended to put there.

So the lesson I've taken is less "assume nothing" — because you can't really do science that way, you need hypotheses — and more "hold your hypotheses loosely and design experiments that could actually tell you you're wrong." A lot of the interpretability work in our group has shifted toward that: rather than going in looking for the representation we think should be there, we try to build tools that let the model tell us what it's representing, and then check whether those explanations are actually causally meaningful, whether intervening on them changes behavior in the predicted way.

And I'd say I still get surprised. Some of the work on in-context learning was like that for me — finding that models were, in some cases, implementing something that looked a lot like a classical learning algorithm, like gradient descent on a linear model, inside the forward pass. I don't think I would have bet on that a priori. But I also try not to over-update on any one finding like that, because the very next model or the very next task might be solved by an entirely different mechanism. So, weak assumptions, strong experiments — that's the aspiration, anyway. Whether I always live up to it is another question.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes loosening their own assumptions from linguistics and symbolic methods, but does not identify freedom from inherited assumptions as an advantage of being a new researcher.

r002.rationale: The candidate favors weak hypotheses and experiments, but does not attribute much of neural sequence modeling’s progress to researchers rejecting the idea that task solving requires a clean, optimal algorithm inside a Transformer.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I've learned that lesson, but I've had to learn it more than once, which probably says something about how strong the pull toward over-assuming actually is.

The pattern for me has usually gone like this. You look at a model doing something that looks like reasoning, or compositional generalization, or following a rule, and the natural move is to reach for the nearest story from linguistics or cognitive science and say, "ah, it's doing that." It has learned the grammar. It has built a world model. It's doing systematic composition. And some of the time that story turns out to be roughly right, and some of the time it turns out the model has found a shortcut that happens to produce the same outputs on your test distribution and falls apart somewhere you didn't think to look.

What's humbling is that the failure usually isn't that the model is dumber than you assumed. Often it's that the model is solving the problem in a way you didn't have a name for. Early on I think a lot of us, myself included, treated "this looks like a symbolic solution" and "this looks like memorization" as the two hypotheses on the table, and the real answer was frequently some third thing, a weird mixture of partial structure and heuristics that doesn't map cleanly onto either.

So the discipline I try to hold onto now is something like: separate the behavioral claim from the mechanistic claim, and be very stingy with the mechanistic one. If I can show that a model generalizes in a certain way under a certain intervention, that's a real finding. If I then say it's because the model represents X, I want to actually go find X, or at least set up the experiment so that the alternative explanations would have produced different results. The interpretability work that's gotten more serious over the last few years has helped a lot here, because it's given us tools to actually check rather than just gesture.

That said, I don't want to overcorrect into total agnosticism either. "Weak assumptions" doesn't mean "no assumptions." Having a hypothesis about what the model is doing is what lets you design a good experiment at all. The trick is to hold it loosely enough that the data is allowed to surprise you, and to notice when you're explaining away a surprise instead of updating on it. I still catch myself doing the former occasionally. So, learned it? Mostly. Finished learning it? Probably not.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve gotten better at it, but I still get surprised. There are really two kinds of assumptions here. One is about what these models are capable of doing, and the other is about how they’re doing it. On the capabilities side, I’ve learned to be cautious about saying, “This is something a neural sequence model just can’t do.” A lot of those claims haven’t aged very well.

But the mechanism question is harder. You see a model succeed at a task, and it’s very tempting to tell a story about the representations it must have built or the procedure it must be following. And often there’s a much simpler way to get the same behavior, especially on the particular distribution you’re evaluating on.

So I try to keep those questions separate: what have we actually demonstrated that the model can do, and what evidence do we have for a particular explanation of how it does it? I don’t think the right response is to stop forming hypotheses. It’s to treat them as hypotheses and look for experiments that could distinguish them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses caution about assumptions, but does not identify freedom from assumptions inherited from prior solutions as an advantage of being a new researcher.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether successful behavior requires a particular mechanism, but does not attribute much of neural sequence modeling’s progress to researchers who avoid assuming Transformers contain clean, optimal algorithms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve gotten better at it, but I’m sure I still have assumptions that are too strong. One thing that keeps happening is that we build a model with some particular story in mind about what it’s going to have to learn, and then we discover that there’s a much simpler way to do well on the task. And the model has found that instead.

So I try to distinguish between what a model’s behavior actually tells us and the explanation we’re tempted to attach to that behavior. If it gets an answer right, that’s evidence that it can get that answer right in that setting. It doesn’t necessarily tell us what representations it has or whether it’ll use the same strategy when we change the setting. Those are separate questions that you have to design experiments to answer.
